opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting claim, but I'd push back on it a bit, or at least say it's incomplete.

Video generation models have clearly learned something about the world. When you watch a generated clip, the lighting looks right, objects mostly stay consistent, things fall downward, water splashes in a plausible way. So there's real knowledge about appearance and dynamics in those weights, and I don't want to dismiss that.

But being able to *render* the world isn't the same as *modeling* it. A video model is fundamentally optimized to produce pixels that look convincing to a human viewer. That's a perceptual objective, not a predictive or causal one. You can generate something that looks right while the underlying physics is wrong, and the model has no incentive to notice, because nobody in the loss function is checking whether the glass actually should have shattered that way.

To me, a world model should let you do a few things. You should be able to intervene: if I take this action, what happens? You should be able to plan: what sequence of actions gets me to some goal? And it should be grounded in a representation that is useful for an agent, not just for a viewer. Most current video models are passive. They watch and continue. They aren't built around action, and they spend huge amounts of capacity on details like texture and pixel-level fidelity that probably don't matter much for reasoning about what's going to happen next.

There's also the question of where the modeling should happen. I lean toward the view that a good world model should operate in a learned representation space rather than pixel space. Pixels are the output we can see, but they're very redundant. Humans don't simulate the future by imagining every pixel; we have a much more abstract sense of objects, space, and cause and effect. So I think the interesting research direction is how to combine the strengths of generative models, their scale and their richness, with representations that are more structured, more spatial, and more action-conditioned.

So my short answer is that video generation is one very important ingredient, and maybe a good stepping stone, but calling it *the* world model is a bit of marketing. The harder and more exciting part is still ahead: going from systems that can paint the world to systems that can understand it and act in it.

r001.rationale: It recognizes that video models learn aspects of the world, but calls them an ingredient and says calling them world models is incomplete and a bit of marketing; it does not clearly endorse that description as reasonable.

r002.rationale: It says video generation is only an ingredient or stepping stone and that the harder work is building systems that understand and act in the world.

r003.rationale: It does not compare video-generation models with language models or describe them as a step beyond language models toward world modeling.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we need to be careful with that claim. Video generation is a very impressive capability, but generating pixels that look plausible is not the same as understanding the world.

When I look at what current video models do, they are extremely good at modeling appearance: textures, lighting, how things look over a few seconds. What they are much weaker at is the stuff you would actually want from a world model: object permanence, consistent physics, counting, keeping track of state when something goes out of frame and comes back. You see a glass fall and the pieces never quite add up. The model is interpolating in pixel space, and pixel space is a very expensive, very noisy place to learn physics.

Part of the problem is the objective. If you train a model to reconstruct every pixel, you spend most of your capacity on things that don't matter for reasoning, like the exact pattern of leaves moving in the wind. A world model, in the sense people like Yann LeCun talk about, should predict in a representation space, abstracting away the irrelevant detail and keeping the structure. That's why I've been pushing on representation learning inside generative models, things like REPA, where you align the diffusion model's internal features with strong self-supervised visual representations. We found that when the model has better representations, generation gets much better and much faster. To me that's evidence that understanding and generation are connected, but understanding is the thing you have to get right first, not something that automatically falls out of generation.

The other missing piece is interaction. A world model is supposed to answer "what happens if I do this." Most video generators are passive; they continue a clip given a text prompt. Without actions and consequences, you have a very good video prior, not a model of the world. Things like Genie are moving in the right direction, but we're early.

So my view is: video generation is a useful stepping stone and a great test bed, and scaling it will keep surprising us. But calling it a world model today is mostly marketing. The honest statement is that these models have learned a lot about how the world looks, and much less about how it works.

r001.rationale: The response calls the world-model label “mostly marketing” today; it does not say the label is reasonable.

r002.rationale: It describes video generation as a stepping stone and says current models are not world models in the fuller sense of modeling how the world works.

r003.rationale: It calls video generation a useful stepping stone, but does not say it advances beyond language models toward world modeling.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by a world model. If we mean a model that learns something about how the world behaves, then video generation is certainly moving in that direction. To predict how a scene changes, you need to capture motion, objects, and some regularities of physical interaction.

But generating a plausible video is not the same as understanding the underlying dynamics. A model can produce something that looks convincing while getting causality wrong. And when it makes a mistake, it can sometimes hide it behind a change in viewpoint or an object disappearing from the scene.

The more interesting question is whether you can use the model to predict the consequences of an action. If I move this object, what happens? If I change the initial conditions, does the prediction change consistently? Can an agent use those predictions to plan? Those are stronger tests than visual quality alone.

So I would treat video generation as a promising route toward world models, but I wouldn’t equate the two. We need to evaluate what these models actually capture about the world, beyond how realistic their outputs look.

r001.rationale: The response says video generation is moving toward models that learn how the world behaves and calls it a promising route toward world models.

r002.rationale: It says video generation should not be equated with world models, but does not specifically reject it as the ultimate form of a world model.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare video-generation models with language models or describe video generation as a step beyond them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by a world model. If we mean a model that captures some regularities of the world—how objects move, how scenes change—then video generation certainly pushes in that direction. To predict what comes next, you need to learn something about how the world works.

But generating a convincing video doesn’t, by itself, demonstrate that you understand the underlying causal structure. A model might produce something visually plausible and still fail on object permanence, physical interactions, or an unusual sequence of events. So I would be careful about equating visual realism with understanding.

The more interesting question is whether that representation can support prediction and action. If I intervene in a scene, can the model predict the consequences consistently? Can an agent use it to plan and accomplish a task? Those are stronger tests than whether a video looks good. I see video generation as a promising route toward world models, but I wouldn’t treat the two as interchangeable.

r001.rationale: It says video generation learns some regularities of the world and “pushes in that direction” toward world models.
